Data Transformations

Author

Danielius Rimas, Kassandra Vroulli, Isabella Braune

Published

October 20, 2026

Project Aim

Het Epos is a primary school which opened in Rotterdam Zuid in 2020. Het Epos aims to demonstrate that differences in learning outcomes are related to pupils’ backgrounds, but importantly also to the quality of education. Within primary education, the school focuses on high-quality teaching, pupil support and parental engagement. The aim of this project is to examine which aspects of early education the school should prioritise to maximise pupils’ development during the kindergarten years and their success throughout the rest of their school career.Specifically, two sub-questions which could be explored are:

1.What effects does spending a longer period in kindergarten have on pupils’ cognitive, social-emotional and executive development, and on their functioning in Years 3 and 4?

In order to examine this question the data will need to contain information pertaining to (a) the amount of years/months children spent in kindergarten, (b) enough variation in terms of how long they spent in kindergarten, to enable a comparison between children who stayed longer, (c) variables that provide information about their cognitive, social-emotional and executive development and lastly (d) information about these pupils that are now in grade 3 or above.

2.What effects does a teaching focus on learning objectives aligned with Years 3 and 4 have on pupils’ academic achievement and subsequent educational pathways? Will need to be examined in a similar manner.

Robustness Checks

Eyebaling the days spent in kindergarten above indicate there are differences in time spent in kindergarten. However, a few assumptions have been made which need to be verified to ensure this is truly representative of their time spent in kindergarten.

Firstly, the variable start_date has now been interperted as the date at which pupils start school. The following checks will therefore be performed, by computing the number of days between the childs 4th birthday and the start date at school. (a) whether the start_date is after the child’s 4th birthday (flag potential mistakes in the data), (b) the child started school no more than 60 days after their birthday (as this school only accepts children that just turned 4), (c) there are no observations before the start date.

Secondly, the time spent in kindergarten has now been estimated from the date at which the last observation was made in grade 1/2 of each pupil. However, if these dates differ significanlty or were registered a long time before the summer holiday (July/ August) we cannot infer how long these children spent in kindergarten. Therefore, the second checks verifies whether the last observation was in july or august (and is not missing).

Thirdly, as a robustness check we can verify whether the pupils current grade year corresponds to the year which they left kindergarten. First by looking at which year the pupil left kindergarten. As school year run from September to August, if the last observation was made between January and August the pupil left kindergarten that year, otherwise the year after. If this calculation is correct, then the expected_end_year should be equal to the end year. Sp for pupils now in grade 4, the end of kindergarten should have been in 2025, and pupils in group 3 2026. e.g. reference year = 2026, current group year = 4 -3 = 1, so ended kindergarten in 2025.

To analyse which pupils fail these checks and why, a table is shown below with which pupils failed which check together with the information which could explain why these checks failed.

Interpertation Robustness checks

The table above shows that there are 25 pupils who did not pass the checks. Firstly, of these pupils, 18 are currently in grade 8. These all failed the check verifying whether the last observation in grade 1/2 was in July or August. The last observation of these pupils were all recorded in december. So either their observations got lost or were not stored correctly. As we are examining development in grades 3:4, we could remove pupils in grade 7 all together to ensure that each grade is represented by an equal amount of students. Secondly, two pupils from grade 5 failed because of NAs and one because the first observation was before the start_date. To ensure we have reliable information these pupils will also not be included in the analysis. The remaining pupils who failed the checks were in group 3 and 4. One because if NAs and in every other case because the pupils should have left kindergarten a year earlier than their current group implies. This could be explained if these pupils had to redo year 3 or 4. These pupils will also not be included in further analysis. Leaving us with a total sample size of N = 79.

RQ1 - Kindergarten duration and functioning in Years 3 & 4

Time spent in Kindergarten and need for extra support

As outlined above, pupils currently in grade 3 till 6, of whom we have observations made in group 1 and 2, and passed all robustness were included in the final sample, resulting in a total sample of 79 students (N).

To determine which developmental outcomes are associated with time spent in kindergarten we will examine the requested support interventions for the selected pupil sample. The data containing information about the support interventions does not contain information about which grade pupils were in when the requests were made. Therefore, the following steps will be taken before analysis this outcome measure.
(1) calculating the grade pupils were in when the request was made (2) filtering out the data of our selected sample

After subselecting the data the following outcomes will be exmained (1) comparison between the number of requested interventions for children who spent an average time in kindergarten (2 years) and those who stayed longer. (2) comparison between the number of support interventions requested and pupils grouped according to how long they spent in kindergarten. (3) examine whetehr a certain need is more common amongst one of these groups

Development Through kindergarten

To operationalize the cognitive, social-emotional and executive development of the pupils, we obtain the scores from the observations from Group1/2 from selected domains. Below are the domains we used to measure each of the three functions. In this analysis, we assume that each objective carries the same weight in measuring the developmental function.

Cognitive Social-emotional Executive development
Auditory development Society Balancing
Numbers Emotional competencies Engagement
Interactive language use Empathy Emotional competencies
Knowledge Self and others Impulse control
Process The space around you Moral competencies
Play Social initiative Task focus and independence
Playing Social autonomy
Counting and number sense Social competencies
Counting and numbers Social flexibility
Visual development Rough-and-tumble play
Well-being

First, we calculate the elapsed time and six-month interval for every observation.

Some pupils have observations recorded at different times of the year. By calculating the elapsed time relative to each pupil’s own start date, we will be able to align the observations by ‘time spent in kindergarten’, rather than by calendar year.

We calculate the average score for each objective, per pupil, per six-month interval. We group observations into six month intervals, to calculate comparable average scores for each pupil and developmental function at successive stages in their kindergarten time.

Then, we calculate the average of the objectives scores per developmental function. We use the average of the objective scores to ensure that each objective received equal weight. ‘n_domain’ records the number of objectives contributing to each function score. We can then investigate if recorded scores tend to improve as time in kindergarten increases.

The plot below addresses the question “How do developmental function scores tend to change as the time since kindergarten entry increases?”

Each thin, grey line represents one pupil, showing for each function how average scores change across every 6 months spent in kindergarten. The blue trend line reflects the overall relationship between time spent in kindergarten and the recorded scores for each function across all pupils. When it rises, the function scores tend to be higher at later intervals (longer period spent in kindergarten).

Next, we visualize how average developmental function scores change over time in kindergarten. Larger points indicate that more pupil observations contributed data.

Finally, we fitted separate mixed-effect models for each function, and adjusted the p-values to account for testing multiple functions.

As shown below, the results suggest that all three functions have a statistically significant positive relationship with kindergarten duration (p values where p<0.05). Cognition has the largest estimated increase (0.195 per 6 months), followed by social-emotional (0.171) and executive development (0.150).

1 Cognitive               0.391 5.89e-40   1.77e-39
2 Executive               0.300 3.40e-28   3.40e-28
3 Social-emotional        0.342 2.89e-36   4.34e-36

Conclusion - Kindergarten duration and developmental functioning

The above analysis suggests that the three development functions (cognitive, social-emotional and executive development), as measured by pupil’s scores in their observations, tend to increase the longer the pupils stay in kindergarten. For every additional 6 months, cognitive function increased by almost 0.2 points, while social-emotional by 0.17 and executive development by 0.15.

The model results showed statistical significance between kindergarten duration and each developmental function, meaning that these relationships are unlikely to be due to random variation alone.

Overall, the findings show that pupils tend to attain higher developmental scores as their time spent in kindergarten increases. It is not proven that this is a causal relationship.

Time spent in kindergarten and functioning in Years 3 & 4

To address the second part of the RQ1, which questions how the duration of kindergarten affects functioning in Years 3 & 4, we first look at the cito test scores from these pupils.

Created by Cito (Central Institute for Test Development), these tests measure primary school pupils’ academic progress throughout the years and help guide their secondary school placement. Here, we will use these test results to reflect their levels of academic achievement in grades 3 and 4.

For our analysis, we retain only pupils in Grades 3 and 4 across all cohorts (2028-2031), and restrict the dataset to pupils included in our for kindergarten analysis. We also select only the tests administered in Grades 3 and 4, excluding tests relevant for later grades (Grade 5 and 6) to ensure consistency and comparability across analyses. We also change performance band “I+” to “I” and “V-” to “V”, as there was only one value of each in the dataset.

We must check if the data have any missing values, and especially if any pupils from the kindergarten duration data are not included in the cito data.

The plot below compares the distribution of the performance bands per test between pupils who spent two years or less in kindergarten, and those who spent more. The results combine all cohorts and assessment periods together.

According to the above visualization, spending longer (more than two years) in kindergarten does not have a consistent advantage in functioning in Years 3 & 4 in terms of Cito test scores. Pupils with longer kindergarten periods show higher performance in TMT, and, to a lesser extent, spelling (non-verbs). However, there is no clear advantage in reading comprehension, while mathematics shows a lowered number of pupils in the top-performing band for longer kindergarten periods. These patterns suggest that any associations between kindergarten duration and Cito test performance are likely subject-specific rather than general.

RQ2: Teaching focus on Year 3 objectives

What effects does a teaching focus on learning objectives aligned with Years 3 and 4 have on pupils’ academic achievement and subsequent educational pathways?

Approach in short

The school has selected 15 learning goals that pupils should reach before they start group 3 (file Selected learning goals.xlsx, sheet 2). For RQ2 we ask: do pupils who mastered more of these goals by the end of kindergarten do better in Year 3 and 4?

Role Variable Source file
Predictor % of the 15 Year 3 goals mastered at the end of kindergarten Observaties_groep_1_2.xlsx
Outcome: achievement Cito scores in Year 3 (mid and end) and Year 4 (end) for Mathematics, TMT (reading speed) and Spelling Cito_UvA_EN.xlsx
Outcome: falling behind Cito performance band IV or V (bottom 40% nationally) Cito_UvA_EN.xlsx
Outcome: keeping up with lessons % of test goals passed in the school’s own maths tests, Year 3 and 4 UvA_testresults_math.xlsx
Outcome: pathway Academic support needed (started or waiting list) and received in Year 3 Support interventions_care team.xlsx
Controls Age at the start of Year 3, cohort (current group) Pupils.xlsx

The steps below are: (1) select pupils, (2) identify the Year 3 goals, (3) clean the observation scores, (4) compute mastery per pupil, (5) build the Cito and support outcomes, (6) combine everything into one dataset, and (7) analyse it.

1. Pupils

We start from the same pupils as RQ1 (pupil_selection, groups 3-7). Unlike RQ1, pupils who failed the kindergarten checks are kept, because repeating a year is itself a possible RQ2 outcome.

The files do not share an ID: the pupil file uses Pupil 002, the support file Leerling 018 and the maths file just 7. Pupil names are unique in the pupil file and appear in every file, so names are used to link the files. str_squish() removes accidental double or trailing spaces so that names match exactly.

2. The Year 3 goals

Sheet 2 of Selected learning goals.xlsx (“Goals before grade one”) lists the 15 goals the school listed as important for a successful start in Year 3. Each goal has a code (e.g. TG11.2_E2) in the same format as the column Leerpadcode in the observations, which is how goals and observations are linked. The sheet has three title rows above the header, hence skip = 3.

Two other options were checked and rejected:

  • Vaktype has a category “check”, but it only covers world orientation, crafts and performing arts, not the Year 3 goals.
  • Leercode is a legacy column: it is filled for almost all rows until 2021/22 and empty from 2024/25 onwards (the school changed its recording system). It is therefore not used, and it is skipped when importing.
[1] 15
[1] 1

All 15 goal codes appear in the observations (share = 1).

3. Cleaning the observation scores

Teachers score each goal on a scale of 0-4, which in practice is 0-3. The score distribution showed:

  • mostly 0, 1, 2 and 3;
  • a few half scores (1.5, 2.5, 3.5), which are kept;
  • 406 scores of 4, which are recoded to 3 (the highest level used in practice);
  • three impossible scores (5 and 22), which are set to missing (NA).

4. Mastery per pupil (the predictor)

A goal is usually observed several times during kindergarten. We want to know where a pupil ended up before Year 3, so for each pupil and goal only the most recent score is kept (arrange(desc(Datum)) puts the latest date first, slice(1) keeps that row).

A goal counts as mastered when that last score is 3 (the highest level). Then, per pupil:

  • n_goals_observed: how many of the 15 goals were observed at all;
  • pct_mastered: mastered goals as a % of all 15 goals (main measure; a goal that was never observed counts as not mastered);
  • pct_mastered_2: the same, but with score 2 or higher counting as mastered (robustness check);
  • pct_of_observed: mastered goals as a % of the goals that were observed (robustness check for pupils with incomplete records).

Table 2 requested by the school

I believe this is what the school asked for: how many goals were designated as important for Year 3, what % of these pupils have mastered on average when starting Year 3, and the lowest and highest values across pupils.

# A tibble: 1 × 6
  n_goals n_pupils mean_pct min_pct max_pct mean_pct_ge2
    <int>    <int>    <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>        <dbl>
1      15      101     67.9    13.3     100         82.9

Interpretation. On average pupils mastered about two thirds (68%) of the 15 goals by the start of Year 3, with large differences between pupils (from 13% to 100%). With the looser definition (score 2 or higher), the average is 83%.

How complete are the records per group?

If a pupil’s record is incomplete, the main measure underestimates their mastery. This table compares the groups.

# A tibble: 5 × 5
  curr_year_group     n mean_goals_observed mean_pct mean_pct_observed
            <dbl> <int>               <dbl>    <dbl>             <dbl>
1               3    26                13.5     66.4              73.2
2               4    29                14.7     74.9              76.5
3               5    15                14.2     66.2              69.8
4               6    14                14.7     84.8              86.4
5               7    17                10.1     45.9              68.3

Interpretation. Groups 3-6 have nearly complete records (13.5-14.7 of the 15 goals observed). Group 7 has on average only about 10 goals observed, and their mastery drops from 68% (of observed goals) to 46% (of all goals): the gap comes from missing observations, not lower mastery. This matches the RQ1 finding that their kindergarten records stop in December. Group 7 is therefore excluded from the outcome analysis.

5a. Outcomes: Cito results

The Cito workbook has one sheet per cohort (CLASS_2028 to CLASS_2031). They are read in and stacked into one table. Some cleaning is needed:

  • Column names are made lower case with underscores (Assessment period -> assessment_period).
  • assessment_period holds two things, e.g. "end 2022-2023". It is split into period (mid/end) and school_year.
  • Which score? The Cito file has four related columns:
Column What it is Comparable between… Used?
score Cito’s ability scale (vaardigheidsscore): correct answers converted to one long scale that runs through primary school, like a height chart. For TMT it is the number of words read correctly in three minutes. Moments within the same test (it rises with age), so progress can be computed. Not between tests: maths and spelling have their own scales. Yes: main outcome, always per test.
ability_score A relative score (0-5): the pupil’s position compared with pupils nationally. Its mean is about 2.2 in every grade, and it rises from band V (mean 1.1) to band I (mean 4.2). Between tests and grades. No: missing for 82% of the Grade 3 results.
performance_band National norm group, I-V, each 20% of pupils: I = top 20%, V = bottom 20%. Based on the score, using the cut-offs in the “Score ranges” sheet. “I+” is treated as I. Between tests and moments. Yes: band IV or V counts as behind.
performance_band_value Meant as the band as a number, but inconsistent (band I has values 2.0-5.0). Not reliable. No.

Band V is by far the most common band at this school, so being “behind” nationally is common here; this is important context for the results.

  • Falling behind. performance_band (I-V) compares a pupil with national norms: I is the top 20%, V the bottom 20%. “I+” is treated as I. Band IV or V counts as behind. The column performance_band_value is inconsistent and is not used.
  • Tests. Only Mathematics, TMT (reading speed) and Spelling (non-verbs) are used, because these were tested in Grade 3 in every school year. Reading Comprehension is missing in Grade 3 for two of the four years.

Repeaters

A pupil with results for the same grade in two different school years has repeated that year. This is checked here because repeating is a possible pathway outcome.

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  repeated_year     n
  <lgl>         <int>
1 FALSE            88
2 TRUE              1

Only one pupil repeated a year. That is too few to analyse, so repeating is reported descriptively but not used as an outcome.

One row per pupil

The Cito data has one row per pupil per test per moment. For the analysis we need one row per pupil, with a column for each test and moment (e.g. score_math_g3_mid = maths score in the middle of Year 3). pivot_wider() does this. For the repeater, only the first attempt is used (arrange(school_year) then slice(1)), because that reflects the level they started Year 3 with.

math_progress is the gain in maths from the middle of Year 3 to the end of Year 4.

5b. Outcomes: support in Year 3

The support file records each referral with the school year (e.g. 2324 = 2023/24), but not the pupil’s group at that time. The group is worked out from the current group:

group at that time = current group - (2026 - start year of that school year)

For example, a pupil now in group 5 was in group 3 in 2024/25.

Choices made:

  • Only support that actually started is counted (Started? = Yes); referrals on the waiting list are not.
  • Academic support means remedial teaching, a language group or 1:1 speech therapy. Motor therapy and behaviour support are less related to being ready in Year 3.
  • The file covers 2023/24 to 2025/26, so Year 3 support is only known for pupils now in groups 4-6. For them, a pupil without a record is assumed to have received no support.

6. Analysis dataset

Everything is joined into one table with one row per pupil in groups 4-6:

  • group 3 is left out because they have no Year 3 Cito results yet;
  • group 7 is left out because their kindergarten records are incomplete.

Two control variables are added:

  • age at the start of Year 3 (Year 3 starts on 1 September of 2026 - (current group - 3));
  • winter birthday (born October-December), a group the school specifically asked about.

7. Analysis

7a. Lower vs higher mastery

As a first, simple comparison, pupils are split at the median of pct_mastered into a “lower” and a “higher” mastery group.

Interpretation. Pupils with higher mastery score higher on all three tests in the middle of Year 3. They are also much less often behind: in maths, roughly 4 in 10 pupils with higher mastery are in band IV/V, compared with roughly 8 in 10 pupils with lower mastery.

7b. Mastery and Year 3 scores

Each dot is a pupil; the black line is a linear fit with its 95% confidence band.

7c. Regression

A linear regression estimates how much the Year 3 score changes per percentage point of mastery, while holding age at the start of Year 3 and cohort constant. Cohort (factor(curr_year_group)) is included because each group took the Year 3 test in a different school year. Pupils with a missing value on any variable in a model are left out of that model.

Interpretation.

  • Mathematics: each extra 10 percentage points of mastery goes with about 11 points higher on the Year 3 mid Cito maths score (b = 1.07 per point, p < .001, n = 57).
  • Spelling: about 12 points higher per 10 percentage points (b = 1.21, p = .002, n = 56).
  • TMT (reading speed): a positive but not significant relation (b = 0.12, p = .13). TMT differs mainly between cohorts, and a few very high scores influence the line.
  • The models explain about a third of the differences between pupils (R² ≈ .34-.36). Age at the start of Year 3 is negatively related to scores, but not significantly.

7d. Robustness checks

Do the maths results depend on the choices made above? Three checks:

  1. a looser definition of mastery (score 2 or higher);
  2. mastery as a % of the goals that were actually observed;
  3. leaving out pupils who are far from the regression line (standardised residual larger than 2.5).

For check 3 the model is first refitted on the pupils without missing values, so that the residuals line up with the right pupils.

7e. Later moments: end of Year 3, end of Year 4 and progress

For reading speed (TMT) there is no relation at any moment. Pupils with higher mastery do not make faster progress in maths from mid Year 3 to end Year 4 (b = 0.24, p = .30): they start Year 3 at a higher level and keep that lead, but the gap does not grow.

In the regression, every 10 percentage points of mastery goes with about 7 percentage points more test goals passed (b = 0.67, p < .001, n = 58, R² = .46). Group 4 pupils also have slightly more Year 3 tests (35 vs 32), probably retakes; this does not affect the percentage passed.

7h. Support in Year 3

Being on the waiting list also shows that the care team saw a need for extra support. We therefore use two measures:

  • support need: referred for academic support in Year 3 (started or on the waiting list);
  • support received: academic support that actually started in Year 3.

A referral counts as academic if the support type is remedial teaching, a language group or speech therapy, or if the need is learning, language or speech & language.

Interpretation. 13 of the 60 pupils (22%) needed academic support in Year 3: 12 received it and 1 was on the waiting list. Pupils who needed support had mastered on average 58% of the Year 3 goals at the end of kindergarten, compared with 80% for pupils who did not need support, a difference of 21 percentage points (95% CI 10-32, t = 4.12, p < .001). Lower mastery at the end of kindergarten thus goes with a higher need for extra support in Year 3. With 13 pupils needing support, this result rests on a small group.

Interpretation. Pupils who spent longer in kindergarten mastered slightly more of the Year 3 goals (r = 0.27). However, mastery still predicts Year 3 results when the time spent in kindergarten is held constant: for Cito maths in the middle of Year 3 (b = 1.01, p < .001, n = 54) and for the share of maths test goals passed in Year 3 (b = 0.57, p < .001, n = 54), close to the estimates without this control (1.07 and 0.67). Time in kindergarten itself is not related to these outcomes once mastery is taken into account (b = -11.5, p = .32 and b = -3.9, p = .54). In other words, what pupils have mastered matters more than how long they stayed in kindergarten; a longer stay seems to help only insofar as it leads to more goals mastered. This links RQ1 and RQ2.

Limitations

  • Association, not effect. Pupils who master more goals may simply be stronger learners; the data cannot separate the effect of teaching from the pupil’s own ability.

  • Mastery, not teaching focus. All pupils received the same kind of teaching; what varies is how much they mastered. Testing the teaching focus itself would require a comparison between groups that were taught differently (e.g. before and after the school introduced the focus, or between classes 1/2a and 1/2b).

  • Small sample (about 60 pupils), from one school.

  • Linking by name. Files are linked on pupil names; a spelling difference would cause a pupil to be missed.

  • Support records. It is assumed that pupils without a record did not need or receive support. Only 13 pupils needed academic support, so this result rests on a small group.

  • Outcomes not available. Repeating a year (only 1 pupil), well-being in Year 3 and the experiences of Year 3-4 teachers (no teacher questionnaire) could not be studied.

    Conclusion RQ2

What we did. For about 60 pupils (current groups 4-6) we measured how many of the 15 goals the school set for the start of Year 3 each pupil had mastered at the end of kindergarten, and related this to their results and support in Years 3 and 4.

What we found.

  • Mastery varies a lot. On average, pupils mastered two thirds (68%) of the goals, ranging from 13% to 100%.
  • Higher mastery goes with better maths and spelling. Pupils who mastered more goals score higher on Cito maths and spelling in Year 3. For maths, this lead is still there at the end of Year 4. For reading speed (TMT) we found no relation.
  • They keep up better with the lessons. In the school’s own maths tests, pupils with higher mastery passed 85% of the Year 3 test goals, compared with 67% for pupils with lower mastery.
  • They fall behind less often. Of the pupils with lower mastery, 64-83% were in the bottom 40% nationally (band IV/V) at each moment, compared with 24-60% of the pupils with higher mastery.
  • They need less extra support. Pupils who needed academic support in Year 3 had mastered 58% of the goals, compared with 80% for the other pupils.
  • They start higher, but do not grow faster. Maths progress from mid Year 3 to end of Year 4 was similar for all pupils: the gap at the start of Year 3 stays, but does not grow.
  • For winter children, mastery matters more than birth month. Pupils born in October-December did worse on average, but this is explained by their lower mastery; at the same mastery level they do as well as other pupils.
    • What pupils master matters more than how long they stay. Pupils who stayed longer in kindergarten mastered slightly more goals, but once mastery is taken into account, time in kindergarten is not related to Year 3 results.

What this means for the school. The 15 goals appear to be a meaningful signal of readiness for Year 3: pupils who reach them start Year 3 at a higher level, keep up better and need less support. Because the gap at the start of Year 3 does not close by itself, monitoring these goals in kindergarten, and giving extra attention to pupils who have not reached them, may be a useful priority.

How certain is this? These are associations in a small group of pupils from one school, not proven effects of the teaching focus. Pupils who master more goals may also be stronger learners in general. To test the teaching focus itself, the school could compare groups taught with and without this focus, for example before and after the focus was introduced.
